The milestone triggered the first royalty payments to Ceres: £110,000 recognised in the 2025 full-year accounts, a sum whose symbolic weight vastly exceeded its nominal value.

The timing aligned with a structural shift in the demand environment that neither Ceres nor Doosan had fully anticipated when they deepened their collaboration. The surge in artificial-intelligence infrastructure investment had created an acute problem for data centre operators: power availability. Doosan Fuel Cell — whose stock gained nearly 25 per cent on the mass-production announcement — had positioned its SOFC systems as a dispatchable, low-emissions on-site generation solution directly competing for data centre backup and primary-power contracts. Caldwell described the convergence bluntly in his year-end statement, noting "unprecedented change in the market with acute demand for power to service AI data centres" arriving precisely as Doosan's production lines came online.

The royalty arithmetic underpinning the 2026-2030 thesis flows directly from this ramp. Analyst estimates at Berenberg suggest that a single licensing partner scaling to 1 GW of annual production under Ceres' Endura technology framework could generate between £50 million and £100 million in annual royalty revenue — a figure that would, at prevailing sector multiples, represent approximately $1 billion in shareholder value creation in isolation. Doosan's 50 MW facility is one fiftieth of that threshold. But it is operating, generating royalties, and targeting the fastest-growing segment of global electricity demand.

## Weichai and the China Manufacturing Licence

On 5 November 2025, Ceres announced the signing of a manufacturing licence agreement with Weichai Power, the Shandong-based diesel engine and powertrain conglomerate that had been a Ceres partner since 2019. The new agreement granted Weichai rights to [produce Ceres SOFC cells and stacks at a dedicated facility in China](https://www.ceres.tech/media/2dtcn4ns/weichai-signs-manufacturing-licence-for-sofc-power-rns.pdf), mirroring the production-scale structure already in place with Doosan in Korea. Ceres retains responsibility for supplying certain proprietary cell components — a design that preserves the technology transfer boundary and keeps royalty economics visible — while receiving upfront licence fees, milestone payments, and ongoing per-unit royalties as production scales.

Licence revenues from the Weichai agreement were guided to begin being recognised in the first half of 2026. The deal addressed a strategic question that the Bosch exit had made more pressing: could Ceres maintain geographic breadth without a German anchor? The answer, partly, was China. Weichai's access to Chinese manufacturing cost structures and distribution in distributed power markets represents a different commercial pathway from the Korean data-centre play, but the royalty mechanics are structurally identical.

## Delta Electronics and the SOEC Dimension

The £43 million Delta Electronics licence signed in January 2024 — Ceres' first explicit hydrogen-electrolysis commercial agreement — moved from deal into product development phase through 2025. Under the agreement, the Taiwanese power electronics manufacturer committed to integrating Ceres' solid oxide electrolyser cell technology with its own thermal management systems at its Tainan manufacturing complex, with [production targeted for commencement by end-2026](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20240118VL207/delta-electronics-ceres-power-hydrogen-energy-fuel-cell.html). Approximately half the £43 million — roughly £21.5 million — was recognised as revenue in 2024; the remainder flows through engineering services and milestone payments as the Tainan line is commissioned.

Delta's entry into the Ceres partner ecosystem was significant beyond its deal value. It was the first licence explicitly spanning both SOFC and SOEC applications, and it came from a manufacturer with established relationships in the data centre power infrastructure market. Delta builds power management systems for some of the largest hyperscale facilities in Asia. The prospect of that distribution network accessing Ceres-derived electrolyser systems — producing green hydrogen for on-site industrial use — extends the potential royalty base beyond stationary power into process chemistry, metals, and heavy transport decarbonisation.

## Shell's Bangalore Milestone

The clearest proof-of-concept for the SOEC pathway came in May 2025, when Shell and Ceres announced that hydrogen was being produced at [Shell's Technology Centre in Bangalore](https://www.ceres.tech/newsroom/news-and-insights/shell-ceres-mw-scale-electrolyser-project-produces-first-hydrogen/) — the site of their joint MW-scale SOEC demonstrator, the first system of its kind operating in India. At full capacity, the electrolyser is capable of producing 600 kilograms of hydrogen per day, with a module-level efficiency of 37 kWh/kg — within range of the EU's stated 2030 target of sub-36 kWh/kg and approximately 35 per cent more hydrogen output per unit of electricity than competing polymer-electrolyte-membrane systems when co-located with industrial heat sources.

The Bangalore demonstrator does not generate royalties. Its function is validation: it establishes that Ceres' metal-supported cell design operates at lower temperatures than conventional solid oxide systems, demonstrating the durability and cost characteristics that would underpin a commercial electrolyser licensing agreement should Shell elect to proceed to production scale. The programme, running since 2022, has systematically de-risked the SOEC technology stack in an operating industrial environment. The question for 2026 and beyond is whether Shell translates demonstrator success into a manufacturing commitment comparable to Doosan's in Korea.

## Centrica, Delta, and the Data Centre Service Model

In March 2026 — just within the chapter's frozen window — Ceres disclosed a strategic partnership with [Centrica](https://www.centrica.com/media-centre/news/2026/centrica-and-ceres-sign-strategic-partnership-to-bring-multi-gw-on-site-fuel-cell-power-to-the-uk-and-europe/), the British energy and services group, targeting multi-gigawatt deployment of on-site fuel cell power across the UK and European market. A subsequent announcement in April 2026 confirmed that Delta Electronics had joined as the manufacturing partner in a three-way structure: Ceres provides technology, Delta manufactures stacks and systems, and Centrica originates projects, handles installation, commissioning, remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, and end-of-life recycling. The model is explicitly service-led — Centrica's energy supply and trading platform absorbs the customer-facing complexity, allowing Ceres and Delta to focus on technology performance.

The data centre application is central to the Centrica-Delta-Ceres thesis. High-density computing facilities require dispatchable power with low grid-dependency, high reliability, and a credible emissions profile. Solid oxide fuel cells — operating on natural gas in the near term, hydrogen-ready as supply chains mature — offer a differentiated proposition against both diesel backup generation and battery storage at the multi-megawatt scale.

## Royalty Geometry and the 2026-2030 Horizon

Ceres enters its 2026-2030 phase with contracted revenue of approximately £45 million before any incremental new business, a cash position of £83.3 million, and a cash outflow that fell to £19.2 million in 2025 from £37.5 million in 2024. The company's gross margin held at 70 per cent on the reduced revenue base, reflecting the structural advantage of a licensing model: when engineering services revenue shrinks, margin does not collapse because the cost base is not vertically integrated against production volumes.

| Partner | Application | Status at May 2026 | Royalty stage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Doosan (Korea) | Stationary power / data centre | 50 MW in mass production | Royalties commenced (£110k, 2025) |
| Weichai (China) | Distributed power | Manufacturing licence signed Nov 2025 | Licence fees H1 2026 → royalties on production |
| Delta Electronics (Taiwan) | SOFC + SOEC / data centre | Product development, production target end-2026 | Engineering milestones → royalties post-2026 |
| Shell (global) | Green hydrogen / SOEC | MW demonstrator producing hydrogen in Bangalore | Pre-commercial; licensing terms unconfirmed |
| Centrica / Delta (UK-Europe) | Data centre / heavy industry | Partnership signed March-April 2026 | Deployment-dependent royalties, medium term |

The transition from fees to royalties will not be smooth. Each partner's ramp follows its own capex cycle, regulatory environment, and end-market demand curve. Doosan's 50 MW facility in Korea is a beginning, not a destination. Weichai's manufacturing line in China is not yet producing cells. Delta's Tainan plant is being commissioned. The Centrica deployment pipeline exists on paper.

But the structure of the 2026-2030 horizon is clearer than at any prior point in Ceres' 25-year history. The company has survived the loss of its most prominent European partner, recognised its first royalties, signed a Chinese manufacturing licence, validated MW-scale electrolysis in a live industrial environment, and entered the data centre market through a three-way commercial model that it could not have assembled without a decade of engineering credibility. Caldwell's framing of 2025 as an inflection year was not investor relations language. It was a description of mechanism: the model is no longer hypothetical. The royalties — all £110,000 of them — have begun.
